caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Equatorial Guinea went from virtually no debt to distress in a decade. At the 2012 oil peak the ratio was just 6.9% of GDP (0.5% in 2008, the series low), and GDP in USD terms hit $22.4bn. As oil fields declined and prices crashed in 2014, revenues collapsed while spending did not: debt climbed to 49.4% of GDP by 2020, the series high, and remains elevated at a projected 40.9% in 2025. A 2018 IMF Staff-Monitored Program pushed for transparency and arrears clearance, but progress has been slow. With oil output in structural decline, the debt path depends on spending restraint the government has historically avoided.
inflation_management: Equatorial Guinea's inflation has been low throughout, anchored by the Central African CFA franc's peg to the euro: it never exceeded 5.7% (2009) and troughed at -0.1% in 2021, averaging around 3%. The peg delivered price stability even as the real economy contracted for most of the 2014-2021 period. But low inflation masked a deep competitiveness problem: with oil declining and the real exchange rate rigid, the non-oil economy has withered, and monetary policy, set regionally by the BEAC, offers no tool for adjustment. Price stability here is the stability of stagnation.

key_events.event: Oil production peaked; GDP hit a series high of $22.4bn; debt was just 6.9% of GDP.
Oil price crash exposed the lack of diversification; the economy entered a multi-year contraction.
IMF Staff-Monitored Program agreed, pressing for governance and oil-revenue transparency.
COVID-19 and a second oil crash pushed debt to 49.4% of GDP, the series high.
Debt remained near 40% of GDP as oil output continued its structural decline.

outlook_next_decade: The base case is managed decline: oil output keeps falling, debt stays elevated, and the CFA peg keeps inflation low while the non-oil economy stagnates. Upside would require genuine diversification or new hydrocarbon finds; downside is a fiscal crisis if spending is not cut as oil revenues fade. Uncertainty is moderate: the regime is stable and the peg credible, but the economic model is exhausted.
